title: Diabetes Can Damage Sight Long Before Symptoms: Why a Retina Check Belongs on Your Calendar
excerpt: Ahead of World Diabetes Day on November 14, Chandigarh Grewal Eye Institute is urging early retina screening. National survey data show 16.9 per cent of Indians with diagnosed diabetes already had some retinopathy — a condition that is painless and often symptom-free until it threatens sight.
body:
• Grewal Eye Institute in Chandigarh is calling for early screening for diabetic retinopathy ahead of World Diabetes Day on November 14 — because the condition damages the retina painlessly and can go unnoticed until sight is already threatened.
  • The scale in India: a national study conducted between 2015 and 2019 found 11.8 per cent of the population lives with diabetes, one in three of them newly diagnosed at the survey itself; among people with diagnosed diabetes, 16.9 per cent had some degree of diabetic retinopathy and 3.6 per cent had a sight-threatening form.
  • The action is simple and specific: if you have type 2 diabetes, get a dilated retina examination at diagnosis and at least once a year after that; bring the date forward if you notice any change in vision.
  • World Diabetes Day 2026-27 theme, set by the International Diabetes Federation, is "Early action on diabetes" — and the eye is where early action pays off most visibly.

The most dangerous thing about diabetic retinopathy is that it does not hurt. The condition is caused by changes in the blood vessels of the retina, the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye, and it is painless: a person can have early retinopathy for a long time without any symptoms, and the changes go unnoticed unless detected by an eye examination, according to Grewal Eye Institute, which has called for early screening ahead of World Diabetes Day on November 14. Gradual, painless blurring of vision is typically the first sign a patient notices — by which point the disease has already progressed.

How big the risk is

The institute notes that the risk of retinopathy rises with the duration of diabetes, and that about 80 per cent of people who have had diabetes for more than fifteen years will have some damage to the blood vessels of the retina. The population numbers point the same way. A national study conducted between 2015 and 2019 found that 11.8 per cent of India population lives with diabetes, and that one in three of those cases was newly diagnosed at the time of the survey — meaning years of undetected high blood sugar. Among people already diagnosed, 16.9 per cent had some degree of diabetic retinopathy and 3.6 per cent had a sight-threatening form, according to the study, reported by The Daily Beat. Clinicians at Delhi Vision Eye Centre have separately warned that about 15 to 20 per cent of their diabetic patients show signs of retinopathy at their very first screening.

What screening actually involves, and when

A screening visit is a dilated eye examination: drops widen the pupil so the retina can be examined directly, because reading an eye chart clearly does not rule out retinal damage. The timing rules are straightforward. People with type 2 diabetes should be screened at diagnosis, since the disease may have been present, unnoticed, for years; people with type 1 diabetes should have their first examination within five years of diagnosis; and everyone with diabetes should repeat the examination at least once a year, and sooner if vision changes. Managing blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol lowers the risk of progression, but it does not replace the examination itself.

Why November 14 is the reminder

World Diabetes Day, observed every year on November 14, carries the 2026-27 theme "Early action on diabetes," set by the International Diabetes Federation, according to Artemis Hospitals. South Asians develop diabetes at a younger age and at a lower body weight, often with more fat around the abdomen — which is why the screening advice applies to diaspora readers in their thirties and forties, not only to older relatives in India. If you have diabetes and cannot remember your last dilated eye examination, that is the finding this article exists to produce: book one.
